title: Machine Learning Prioritizes Candidate Viral Sequences in Pediatric Plasma
excerpt: Tree-based machine learning prioritized candidate viral sequences within unclassified plasma metagenomic data from pediatric febrile neutropenia patients, identifying biologically supported
content:
Computational researchers applying supervised machine learning to unresolved metagenomic sequencing data have demonstrated a method to identify and prioritize candidate viral sequences from clinical plasma samples. Metagenomic shotgun sequencing provides an untargeted window into microbial populations by sequencing genetic material directly from host specimens without requiring prior knowledge of specific microbial targets. Despite the analytical reach of next-generation sequencing, a substantial proportion of recovered reads routinely escapes classification against reference databases, forming an unresolved sequence fraction often designated as metagenomic or viral dark matter. In clinical cohorts, these unassigned sequences can reflect technical artifacts, degraded background nucleic acids, or highly divergent viral lineages that diverge markedly from cataloged reference genomes. In a study published in Frontiers in Bioinformatics, investigators examined whether tree-based machine learning architectures could systematically parse this unclassified fraction recovered from the plasma of pediatric patients experiencing febrile neutropenia.

The study reanalyzed publicly available metagenomic datasets generated from plasma collected from fifteen pediatric patients presenting with febrile neutropenia of unknown etiology at the University Hospital of the Ribeirão Preto Medical School, University of São Paulo. Febrile neutropenia presents an important immunological context for virome exploration, as underlying immunosuppression and continuous antigenic exposure can permit opportunistic, divergent, or poorly characterized viruses to persist at detectable systemic levels. Following standard preprocessing procedures, which included quality inspection, adapter trimming, read filtering, and the computational depletion of host-derived sequences aligned against the human reference genome GRCh38.p14, initial taxonomic profiling was conducted using Kraken2 against the NCBI RefSeq and SILVA databases. This conventional classification step assigned 45.02 percent of the dataset, representing 9,618,246 reads, to viral taxa, while bacterial reads constituted 11.78 percent, and eukaryotic and archaeal reads accounted for 0.75 percent and 0.0125 percent, respectively. Strikingly, 42.4 percent of the sequencing reads, amounting to 9,068,122 reads, remained completely unclassified, providing the primary substrate for subsequent de novo assembly and machine learning evaluation.

To extract cohesive genetic fragments from this unresolved pool, the unclassified reads were assembled de novo using metaSPAdes across multiple k-mer dimensions of 21, 33, 55, and 77. This multi-k-mer strategy was implemented to accommodate varying biological constraints, leveraging smaller k-mers to capture low-abundance viral sequences while utilizing larger k-mers to resolve repetitive regions and preserve contig continuity. Assembly yielded 8,640 contigs exceeding a length threshold of 500 nucleotides. However, the machine learning models utilized in the study relied on predictive features that incorporated protein domain similarity scores alongside sequence-derived composition statistics. Consequently, contigs were subjected to a filtering criterion requiring the presence of at least one protein profile represented within the training space. Only 149 of the 8,640 contigs, representing 1.72 percent of the assembled set, met this eligibility requirement, whereas 8,491 contigs, or 98.28 percent, were excluded from downstream machine learning classification due to the absence of compatible protein profiles.

The two supervised classification architectures evaluated in the investigation were Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting, commonly designated as XGBoost. Both tree-based frameworks were trained using a curated collection of 70,799 complete viral genomes retrieved from the NCBI Virus database, restricted strictly to Homo sapiens hosts across 34 viral families. Feature extraction captured intrinsic sequence properties, such as guanine-cytosine content, sequence length, and the complete spectrum of 256 possible tetranucleotide frequencies, which serve as functional and phylogenetic genomic signatures. In addition, translated amino acid sequences were screened against the Pfam-A and vFam Hidden Markov Model databases using HMMER v3.4 to derive bit scores representing similarity to known viral protein domains. The reference dataset was split into stratified subsets, allocating 75 percent, or 53,099 genomes, to model training and cross-validation, and retaining 25 percent, or 17,700 genomes, as an entirely independent held-out test set.

Internal model validation demonstrated high predictive capacity when evaluated on curated, complete reference genomes. When evaluated against the held-out test set of 17,700 complete viral genomes, Random Forest attained an overall accuracy of 0.9989, balanced accuracy of 0.986519, macro precision of 0.980725, macro recall of 0.986519, macro F1-score of 0.983255, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.998840. XGBoost yielded an accuracy of 0.9988, balanced accuracy of 0.981814, macro precision of 0.985597, macro recall of 0.981814, macro F1-score of 0.982881, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.998718. Paired bootstrap resampling across 5,000 stratified iterations demonstrated that the 95 percent confidence intervals for performance differences between the two models spanned zero across all evaluated metrics, and an exact McNemar test confirmed no statistically significant divergence in paired classification outcomes on the reference data.

Analysis of feature importance revealed distinct mathematical priorities between the two tree-based models. Within the Random Forest framework, the highest normalized importance was assigned to the RNA helicase domain PF00910 with a mean decrease impurity of 0.013, followed by contig sequence length with a normalized value of 0.85 and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase domain PF00680 with a normalized value of 0.77. In contrast, XGBoost placed its highest emphasis on specific protein domains, headed by the viral DNA polymerase C-terminal domain PF00336 with a mean decrease impurity of 0.11 and the retroviral envelope glycoprotein domain GP120 PF00516 with a normalized value of 0.75. These rankings confirmed that the models captured established functional markers of viral replication and structure, although the relative contribution of each feature remained specific to the individual algorithm.

When deployed on the 149 clinical contigs recovered from plasma dark matter, the classifiers exhibited moderate concordance, characterized by an overall Cohen’s kappa coefficient of 0.49 across the retained sequences. XGBoost distributed contigs across ten viral families, while Random Forest assigned them across nine families, with the two models demonstrating strong mutual convergence primarily for Anelloviridae, encompassing 69 concordant contigs, and Sedoreoviridae, encompassing 32 concordant contigs. In total, 91 of the 149 evaluated contigs, or 61.1 percent, were classified as members of the Anelloviridae family by at least one of the algorithms. Independent biological validation through BLASTx queries against the NCBI non-redundant database and protein domain profiling confirmed canonical anellovirus architecture in 78 of these 91 contigs, identifying characteristic conserved domains such as TT_ORF1 in 61.5 percent, DUF755 in 33.3 percent, TT_ORF2 in 24.4 percent, and TT_ORF2a in 6.4 percent of cases.

Conversely, contigs assigned to taxonomic families other than Anelloviridae, totaling 58 sequences, universally lacked corroborating biological evidence. Predictions in this non-anellovirus group generally lacked family-specific protein profiles and failed to match corresponding viral taxa in sequence homology searches. A prominent example of this limitation occurred within the Sedoreoviridae family, to which 62 contigs were assigned across models despite an absence of matching domain architectures or BLASTx support. Because both algorithms operated within a closed taxonomic space comprising 34 viral families without an explicit negative or non-viral class, divergent or low-information sequences were forced into represented categories. The authors noted that Sedoreoviridae appeared to act as an attractor class within the learned feature space, capturing fragmented or ambiguous inputs that could not be classified as unknown by the supervised models.

Among the biologically supported Anelloviridae contigs, phylogenetic reconstruction was conducted using open reading frame 1 sequences predicted by Prodigal. Following the removal of 28 redundant, identical sequences recovered from a single patient sample, 44 non-redundant ORF1 sequences were aligned with 86 reference proteins from the SCANellome dataset representing recognized human anellovirus genera. Phylogenetic inference using IQ-TREE under the GTR+F+ASC+R6 substitution model distributed the sequences across multiple lineages, placing 22 contigs within Alphatorquevirus, 19 within Betatorquevirus, two within Gammatorquevirus, and one sequence from sample FN14 within the recently established genus Samektorquevirus. This sequence, designated NODE_3, exhibited 95 percent pairwise nucleotide identity to the reference genome MN779243.1, substantially exceeding the 69 percent species demarcation threshold established by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses and confirming its assignment to the species Samektorquevirus hominid 15.

The authors emphasized key limitations inherent to the methodology, noting that the models were trained exclusively on full-length viral genomes but applied to fragmented metagenomic contigs that frequently contained incomplete coding sequences. Furthermore, the exclusion of 98.28 percent of assembled contigs due to the absence of recognizable protein domains underscores that tree-based models operating on defined viral feature sets cannot prioritize completely novel or unrecognizable genetic entities. The researchers cautioned that computational taxonomic prioritization does not establish active viral replication, clinical pathogenicity, or disease causality in febrile neutropenia, concluding that such machine learning frameworks serve as complementary prioritization tools that require independent molecular and phylogenetic confirmation.

Subject of Research: Prioritizing candidate viral sequences in unclassified pediatric plasma metagenomes using tree-based machine learning

Article Title: Tree-based machine learning prioritizes candidate viral sequences in human plasma metagenomic dark matter
